paragraphs: Learning a Bayesian network means choosing directed relationships among variables while ensuring that those relationships never form a directed cycle. For continuous variables in high dimensions, the number of possible networks makes this difficult. A common approach first removes candidate relationships and then searches the remaining possibilities, but this early pruning can discard the correct structure.

A* lasso combines structure selection and the acyclicity requirement within a single optimization problem. It uses A* search to explore network structures and incorporates lasso into the scoring system to favor sparse networks. This connects the search for a valid directed graph with the preference for relatively few relationships, instead of handling them in separate stages.

The authors report that the method recovers the optimal sparse structure for its optimization problem while substantially improving computational efficiency over exact dynamic programming methods. They also introduce a faster heuristic version. Evaluations on benchmark networks and real data show further efficiency improvements without a significant loss in solution quality.
neurips-2013-a-lasso-for-learning-a-spar.tldr: A* lasso combines sparse network scoring with graph search to learn optimal Bayesian network structures more efficiently.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether competition between neighboring neurons can improve artificial neural networks. Such local competition is common in biological networks. The authors bring this idea into artificial networks with multiple layers, trained using gradients and backpropagation, so competition becomes part of a familiar learning framework.

The central comparison is between networks containing competing linear units and networks containing non-competing nonlinear units. This changes how units interact as well as the kind of units being used. The reported tendency is that networks with competing linear units perform better. That wording supports competition as a promising design choice, without establishing that it wins for every network or learning problem.

The authors also report that these networks avoid catastrophic forgetting when training sets change over time. Catastrophic forgetting refers to losing previously learned behavior while learning from new data. This finding gives the architectural idea a second motivation: competition may help a network retain earlier learning while its training experience changes, alongside its reported performance benefits.
neurips-2013-compete-to-compute-21b197ef.tldr: Multilayer networks with competing linear units tend to outperform non-competing nonlinear networks and are reported to avoid catastrophic forgetting.

paragraphs: DirectBoost builds an ensemble by combining weak classifiers, with training organized around two objectives. First, it directly reduces the number of incorrectly classified training examples. This is empirical classification error, also called 0–1 loss, because each example contributes according to whether its predicted label is wrong.

The first phase uses greedy coordinate descent and stops at a local coordinatewise minimum. The algorithm then switches to greedy coordinate ascent, continuing to add weak classifiers while increasing a chosen margin objective. Margins describe how strongly examples are classified. The framework permits arbitrarily defined target margins, but its stopping claim concerns a local coordinatewise maximum in the authors' specified sense, rather than a global optimum.

Across a collection of benchmark datasets, the authors report consistently better results than AdaBoost, LogitBoost, LPBoost with column generation, and BrownBoost. They also report noise tolerance when optimizing a particular ordered bottom-sample margin. That qualification matters: the stated noise result is tied to the selected margin objective, not every possible margin definition.
neurips-2013-direct-0-1-loss-minimizatio.tldr: DirectBoost first greedily minimizes training classification error, then improves chosen margins, with favorable benchmark results and qualified noise tolerance.

paragraphs: A statistical model can contain several kinds of structure at once. This paper studies parameters represented as a sum of components, each subject to its own structural constraint. The term “dirty” describes this combination of structures: the overall parameter need not fit a single structural description even when its individual components do.

The authors develop a unified framework for analyzing these models in high dimensions. Their estimators combine a loss function with a hybrid regularizer built from weighted penalties for the separate components. Technically, the hybrid penalty is an infimal convolution: it considers ways to split a parameter into components and uses the least total weighted penalty across those splits.

The framework allows any number and types of structures and accommodates different statistical models and loss functions. Corollaries demonstrate its application to linear regression, multiple regression, and principal component analysis with varied superpositions. The contribution is a common analytical treatment of these combinations, allowing structurally different estimation problems to be studied through the same framework.
neurips-2013-dirty-statistical-models-e4.tldr: The paper provides a unified framework for analyzing statistical models whose parameters combine multiple separately constrained structures.

paragraphs: Counting grids represent documents using a spatial arrangement of word distributions. A document's word counts are modeled by combining the histograms inside a window on that grid. This captures the observation that documents in many collections can change smoothly into one another as some words disappear and others enter.

The original approach requires all of a document's content to come from one contiguous grid region. That restriction can be problematic, particularly when the grid has few dimensions. The proposed Componential Counting Grid allows a document to draw on multiple windows, bringing the ability to combine separate components from topic models into the grid representation.

The authors also construct a generative kernel from how documents use the grid and introduce a visualization approach for understanding large text collections. These additions make the representation useful beyond fitting word counts. Evaluations on document classification and multimodal retrieval report state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks, supporting the practical value of allowing multiple regions to contribute to a document.
neurips-2013-documents-as-multiple-overl.tldr: Componential Counting Grids model documents with multiple grid windows, improving flexibility and achieving strong classification and retrieval results.

paragraphs: Tensor completion seeks to recover a multidimensional array from only some of its entries. The paper focuses on pairwise interaction tensors, a structured family used to model data with multiple attributes. This narrower setting is central: the authors describe efficient, guaranteed recovery of general tensors from limited observations as unlikely.

Their recovery method solves a constrained convex optimization problem that minimizes a weighted sum of matrix nuclear norms. In the noiseless setting, they prove exact recovery from O(nr log²(n)) observations. For noisy observations, they analyze a constrained convex program and establish error bounds, replacing exact reconstruction with a quantified statement about recovery accuracy.

Synthetic experiments show recovery behavior that agrees well with the theoretical analysis. The method also achieves state-of-the-art results on a temporal collaborative filtering task. Together, these findings connect a tractable optimization procedure with both recovery guarantees for the studied tensor family and evidence of usefulness in a recommendation setting involving time.
neurips-2013-exact-and-stable-recovery-o.tldr: A convex recovery method provides exact noiseless recovery and noisy error bounds for pairwise interaction tensors, with supporting experiments.

paragraphs: Estimating a covariance matrix involves learning how variables vary together. Analytic shrinkage regularizes that estimate and offers a fast alternative to choosing regularization through cross-validation. The paper revisits the theoretical consistency of this approach, examining what its supporting proof actually requires of the covariance matrix.

The authors show that the existing consistency argument implies restrictions on how eigenvalues grow and how dispersed they can be. These restrictions are often violated in data. They then prove consistency under assumptions that do not constrain the covariance structure. This broadens the structural scope of the guarantee while retaining an assumption-based theoretical result.

The paper also introduces orthogonal complement shrinkage, an extension designed to adapt to covariance structure. Evaluations cover finance, spoken-letter recognition, optical character recognition, and neuroscience, with superior performance reported for the new approach. The work therefore contributes both a revised foundation for analytic shrinkage and an adaptive method whose benefits are demonstrated across several kinds of data.
neurips-2013-generalizing-analytic-shrin.tldr: The paper broadens consistency guarantees for analytic covariance shrinkage and introduces a structure-adaptive extension with improved empirical performance.

paragraphs: Local learning predicts an outcome from nearby data points. The paper asks how this idea should work when several tasks are learned together. It departs from neighborhoods containing examples from only one task and instead forms neighborhoods using data points from all tasks, creating a direct route for sharing information locally.

For classification, the authors extend the k-nearest-neighbor rule so that neighbors from different tasks contribute through task-specific voting weights. They introduce a regularizer that encourages the task-weight matrix to be close to symmetric, and develop an efficient coordinate descent algorithm for the resulting objective. The weighting mechanism lets contributions depend on task relationships rather than treating all neighboring points identically.

For regression, the paper extends kernel regression using the same general strategy of neighborhoods spanning tasks. Experiments on toy data and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods. The contribution is a way to combine the local character of neighborhood prediction with explicit, learned weighting of information from multiple tasks.
neurips-2013-heterogeneous-neighborhood-.tldr: The proposed classification and regression methods share information through neighborhoods spanning multiple tasks, using task-specific weights.

paragraphs: Optimizing an unknown function is difficult when it has many inputs and each noisy evaluation is expensive. This paper assumes that the function actually changes only along a low-dimensional subspace. It also assumes smoothness, expressed through a low norm in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. These conditions provide structure that the optimization algorithm can exploit.

The proposed SI-BO algorithm first uses ideas from low-rank matrix recovery to learn the relevant subspace. It then uses Gaussian Process Upper Confidence sampling to optimize the function. The sampling budget must serve both purposes: discovering which directions matter and finding good function values within those directions.

The authors analyze this allocation to balance exploration and exploitation. Under the stated setting, they obtain subexponential cumulative regret bounds and convergence rates for high-dimensional Bayesian optimization with noisy observations. Numerical results demonstrate effectiveness in difficult scenarios. The result shows how learning a smaller underlying search space can make a structured high-dimensional optimization problem more manageable.
neurips-2013-high-dimensional-gaussian-p.tldr: SI-BO learns a low-dimensional active subspace and optimizes within it, with guarantees under stated subspace and smoothness assumptions.

paragraphs: A single image contains intertwined evidence about a scene's shape, reflectance, illumination, objects, and materials. Recovering these properties is challenging because the visible image reflects their combined effects. The paper explores whether estimating them together can exploit relationships that would be missed when the tasks are handled separately.

The authors formulate a joint energy minimization problem. This provides a shared objective for intrinsic scene properties, object identities such as tables and monitors, and material attributes such as wood and plastic. By encoding correlations among these quantities, the model allows evidence about one aspect of a scene to help constrain estimates of the others.

The motivation includes moving beyond the laboratory datasets used by many earlier intrinsic-image models. Tests on the NYU and Pascal datasets show both qualitative and quantitative improvements in overall accuracy. These results support the proposed synergy between physical scene interpretation and object or material recognition: their relationships can be useful information within a single estimation framework.
neurips-2013-higher-order-priors-for-joi.tldr: Jointly estimating intrinsic scene properties, objects, and materials improves overall accuracy by modeling their correlations.

paragraphs: Lasso finds sparse regression representations, but solving it can be expensive when both the sample count and feature count are very large. Screening reduces this burden by identifying predictors whose final coefficients will be zero. Those predictors can then be removed before solving the smaller optimization problem.

The proposed Dual Polytope Projection rule uses the geometry of lasso's dual formulation. In that formulation, certain inactive constraints identify predictors that can be excluded. The feasible region is a closed convex polytope, which gives the relevant projection uniqueness and nonexpansiveness. These properties constrain where the optimal dual solution can lie and support efficient decisions about which predictors are inactive.

The authors also extend the approach to identifying inactive groups in group lasso, where screening removes groups of predictors together. Across many real datasets, the rule identifies more inactive predictors than existing state-of-the-art lasso screening rules. Its practical value lies in shrinking the optimization problem through mathematically supported exclusions, allowing the solver to concentrate on the remaining features.
neurips-2013-lasso-screening-rules-via-d.tldr: Dual Polytope Projection uses lasso's dual geometry to screen out zero-coefficient predictors and extends to inactive groups in group lasso.

paragraphs: Invariance information describes how a prediction should behave when an input changes in a relevant way. This paper incorporates local invariances into learning in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The focus is on specifying the target function's behavior around individual data instances, giving the learner information beyond the observed examples themselves.

The authors encode this information compactly through linear functionals and penalize their values with a loss function. They establish a representer theorem that makes the formulation efficiently optimizable as a convex program. This addresses computational difficulties associated with earlier approaches, including expensive optimization, reliance on separation oracles, and non-convex formulations.

The theorem requires the linear functionals to be bounded in the chosen function space. The authors show that this requirement holds for a variety of commonly used spaces and invariances. Experiments involving unlabeled data and transformation invariances produce results better than or similar to the state of the art, supporting the framework's combination of expressiveness and tractable optimization.
neurips-2013-learning-with-invariance-vi.tldr: The framework encodes local invariances as linear functionals, enabling convex kernel learning when the required boundedness condition holds.

paragraphs: A marginal distribution describes only part of a collection of variables, whereas a joint distribution describes them together. This paper studies computational connections between problems involving marginals and inference problems in models that specify a full joint distribution. Its aim is to show when methods for one kind of problem can help solve another.

The authors prove general, efficient reductions among several classical and new problems. A reduction translates the task being solved into calls to another computational problem. Their results show that advances in model-based inference can automatically yield advances for the corresponding “pure data” problems connected by these reductions.

The main construction expresses problems as linear programs and uses the target problem to provide a dual separation oracle for the Ellipsoid Method. In this role, the target computation supplies the information needed by the optimization procedure. Beyond the individual reductions, the authors suggest that this technique may have independent value for probabilistic inference, offering a reusable way to establish computational relationships.
neurips-2013-marginals-to-models-reducib.tldr: Efficient reductions connect marginal-distribution problems to joint-model inference, allowing algorithmic advances to transfer between them.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether additional training examples can reduce the computation needed to learn, even after enough examples are available statistically. It studies agnostic PAC learning of halfspaces over vectors in {-1, 0, 1}ⁿ with at most three nonzero coordinates. This provides a concrete supervised learning setting for separating data requirements from computational requirements.

The class can be learned using O(n/ε²) examples by an inefficient procedure. Under the assumption that refuting random 3CNF formulas is hard, the authors show that efficient learning with that sample count is impossible. Stronger hardness assumptions extend the obstruction even to O(n^1.499/ε²) examples. These are conditional computational lower bounds.

The positive result is an efficient algorithm using roughly n²/ε² examples, with logarithmic factors suppressed in the stated sample scale. Together, the results establish a tradeoff: a larger dataset can enable efficient computation for this problem. The paper also introduces a non-cryptographic methodology for proving such gaps between statistical feasibility and computational efficiency.
neurips-2013-more-data-speeds-up-trainin.tldr: For a sparse halfspace learning problem, more examples enable efficient learning while smaller sample regimes are computationally hard under stated assumptions.

paragraphs: Predicting a response can require more than estimating its average. Its variability and the shape of its distribution may also change with the input features. This paper develops a model for estimating that entire conditional distribution when the feature space is extremely large, allowing these different aspects of the response to vary flexibly.

The model represents each conditional density as a weighted combination of dictionary densities, with nonnegative weights that sum to one. Which densities are used, and how much each contributes, depend on a path through a tree decomposition of the feature space. A fast graph partitioning algorithm builds this tree, providing the multiscale organization.

Bayesian methods then prune the tree adaptively and average probabilistically over different subtrees. This allows the model to combine alternatives instead of relying on one fixed tree resolution. The algorithm scales to approximately one million features, and the authors report state-of-the-art predictive performance on toy examples and two neuroscience applications, including settings at that feature scale.
neurips-2013-multiscale-dictionary-learn.tldr: A tree-organized dictionary of densities estimates flexible conditional distributions and scales to approximately one million features.

paragraphs: Proximal maps are central operations in gradient-type optimization algorithms used for large, high-dimensional problems. For a simple function, the operation may have a direct closed-form solution. Once several regularizers are combined to encourage different structures simultaneously, the corresponding operation can become much harder to compute.

The paper investigates when the proximal map for a sum of functions can be obtained by composing the individual proximal maps. In practical terms, it asks when a difficult combined operation can be replaced exactly by a sequence of simpler operations. The question is about identifying valid decompositions; the paper does not claim that arbitrary sums permit this replacement.

The authors develop a systematic theory that brings together several previously scattered results and yields additional decompositions with little extra effort. This matters because a structural understanding of when decomposition works can make combined regularizers easier to handle. The contribution is a framework for recognizing these opportunities, linking the design of structured penalties to the operations required by optimization algorithms.
neurips-2013-on-decomposing-the-proximal.tldr: The paper develops a theory for when the proximal map of a sum can be computed by composing simpler proximal maps.

paragraphs: Bayesian nonparametric mixture models offer flexibility, but expensive inference can make them difficult to use on large datasets. This paper addresses that computational obstacle for Dirichlet process mixture models. The goal is to estimate the model progressively as data are processed, while allowing additional mixture components to appear when needed.

The algorithm begins with a specified prior and recursively transforms it into an approximate posterior through sequential variational approximation. It departs from a workflow based on random initialization followed by repeated updates. New components are incorporated during the sequential procedure, so the evolving approximation can expand its representation as learning proceeds.

The authors report that the algorithm can reliably estimate a Dirichlet process mixture model in a single pass, making it particularly suitable for massive datasets. Experiments on synthetic and real data show speedups of orders of magnitude over state-of-the-art methods. The main practical finding is that progressive approximate inference can substantially reduce the computational burden of fitting this flexible model family.
neurips-2013-online-learning-of-nonparam.tldr: Sequential variational approximation fits Dirichlet process mixtures in one pass, adding components as needed and delivering large experimental speedups.

paragraphs: Robust principal component analysis seeks an underlying subspace while accounting for sparse corruption in the observations. Typical batch methods require loading all samples into memory, which hinders their use on large datasets. This paper develops an online method that handles one sample at a time, so memory cost does not grow with the number of samples.

The proposed OR-PCA algorithm uses stochastic optimization of a reformulation equivalent to the batch robust PCA problem. The authors show that its sequence of subspace estimates converges to the optimum of its batch counterpart. This connection supplies a theoretical basis for robustness to sparse corruption, linking the online computation to the batch objective.

The method can also be used to track a subspace that changes over time. Simulations examine both subspace recovery and tracking, demonstrating robustness and efficiency advantages over online PCA and batch robust PCA methods. The contribution combines reduced storage requirements with a convergence result and evidence that the online formulation is useful for evolving data.
neurips-2013-online-robust-pca-via-stoch.tldr: OR-PCA processes samples individually, converges to its batch counterpart's optimum, and supports robust subspace recovery and tracking.

paragraphs: Structured sparse estimation encourages a model to use relatively few components while respecting additional organization. Such regularization is useful in data analysis, but the resulting optimization problems often demand sophisticated algorithms. This paper looks for a computational route that makes a broad class of these estimators easier to train.

The authors identify a rich class of structured sparse regularizers whose polar operators can be computed efficiently. That operator supplies a key operation for a simple conditional gradient method. Combined with smoothing and local optimization, the resulting approach significantly reduces training time compared with the state of the art, according to the reported findings.

The paper also establishes a reduction from polar computations to proximal maps and uses it to enable more efficient latent fused lasso. This provides another connection between the regularizer's mathematical structure and an available optimization operation. The broader contribution is to identify efficiently computable building blocks that can support simpler training methods for otherwise computationally demanding structured estimators.
neurips-2013-polar-operators-for-structu.tldr: Efficient polar operators enable faster conditional gradient methods for structured sparsity, with a further reduction benefiting latent fused lasso.

paragraphs: Electrophysiology recordings contain signals from multiple neurons. A traditional analysis first thresholds waveforms to identify possible spikes and then clusters those waveforms into individual neurons. This paper combines detection and clustering within a Gamma process model, extending earlier Bayesian nonparametric approaches to neural spiking.

The authors develop an online approximate inference procedure that enables real-time analysis and reports performance beyond the previous state of the art. Their model accounts for colored noise, detects overlapping spikes, tracks changes in waveforms, and uses multiple recording channels. These features address several aspects of the recorded signals within the same inference framework.

Exploratory analyses use data with partial ground truth and two new datasets. The authors find that the listed model features collectively contribute to improved performance, supporting their combined use rather than attributing the gains to a single feature. They present experiments measuring thousands of neurons and dynamically adapting stimuli as future possibilities they hope to enable, rather than capabilities already demonstrated by the reported analysis.
neurips-2013-real-time-inference-for-a-g.tldr: An online Gamma process model jointly detects and clusters neural spikes, enabling real-time analysis with improved reported performance.

paragraphs: The paper studies principal component regression, which uses principal-component structure in a regression problem. Its first contribution concerns the Gaussian setting in low dimensions, within an asymptotic framework where both dimension and sample size can increase. Using developments in minimax-optimal principal component estimation, the authors sharply characterize when classical principal component regression can offer an advantage over least squares.

The second contribution is a robust sparse method for high-dimensional data following an elliptical distribution. This family generalizes the Gaussian model and includes distributions such as multivariate t and Cauchy. It can accommodate heavy tails and tail dependence, making the modeling assumptions relevant to financial and biomedical imaging data.

Under the elliptical model, the authors prove that their method can estimate regression coefficients at the optimal parametric rate. This supplies theoretical support for an alternative to Gaussian-based methods in the studied setting. Experiments on synthetic and real data illustrate empirical usefulness, complementing the analysis of both classical principal component regression and the new robust sparse estimator.
neurips-2013-robust-sparse-principal-com.tldr: The paper characterizes potential advantages of principal component regression and develops a robust sparse estimator with optimal-rate guarantees under an elliptical model.

paragraphs: Influence estimation asks how widely information can spread through a network within a specified time. The time limit is part of the problem: eventual reach alone does not answer how much spreading occurs soon enough. This paper proposes a randomized estimation algorithm for networks with continuous-time diffusion.

The algorithm estimates influence for every node to accuracy ε using O(1/ε²) randomizations. Up to logarithmic factors, its computation is linear in the number of nodes and edges multiplied by the number of randomizations. This ties the cost of increased accuracy to an explicit sampling requirement while keeping the dependence on network size scalable.

Used inside greedy influence maximization, the estimator yields a selected set with influence at least (1 − 1/e)OPT − 2ε, where OPT is the optimal value. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data scale to millions of nodes and improve both estimated influence accuracy and the quality of selected nodes over previous state-of-the-art approaches. The work connects efficient estimation with a quantified selection guarantee.
neurips-2013-scalable-influence-estimati.tldr: A randomized method estimates time-sensitive network influence at large scale and supports greedy node selection with an approximation guarantee.

paragraphs: Randomized methods can accelerate regression, and this paper investigates how to extend their benefits to structured nonlinear lₚ regression problems. The focus is on problems involving Vandermonde matrices. These matrices arise in polynomial fitting and in randomized techniques for making kernel methods scalable, connecting the analysis to several statistical modeling settings.

The main idea is to exploit the matrix's structure when accelerating the regression computation. Treating a structured matrix as a generic collection of entries can overlook opportunities supplied by its organization. The authors show that exploiting this organization produces running times faster than input sparsity, the benchmark associated with the number of nonzero entries in the matrix.

That speed claim is established for the structured regression problems considered in the paper. Empirical results support both the practical usefulness of the modeling framework and the speed benefits of randomized regression. The contribution is therefore a combination of structured modeling and faster computation: the same mathematical form that defines the regression problem also enables additional algorithmic savings.
neurips-2013-sketching-structured-matric.tldr: Exploiting Vandermonde structure accelerates randomized nonlinear regression beyond input-sparsity running times in the studied problem class.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the transition between two stages of training deep belief networks: unsupervised learning and strongly discriminative optimization. The authors propose a three-phase procedure that adds a bridge between them. Its purpose is to connect the learning signals used across the training process more closely.

Their implementation regularizes deep belief networks using top-down information. The network is assembled from restricted Boltzmann machines trained with a combination of bottom-up and top-down sampled signals. A global optimization procedure merges samples from a forward bottom-up pass with samples from a top-down pass, allowing both directions to participate in learning the network.

Experiments on MNIST show improvements over existing deep belief network algorithms. On Caltech-101, the method produces competitive object-recognition results. These are distinct empirical claims: the abstract reports improvement in the first setting and competitiveness in the second. Together, they support the usefulness of introducing top-down regularization into a staged training procedure for the deep belief networks studied.
neurips-2013-top-down-regularization-of-.tldr: A three-phase training procedure uses top-down signals to regularize deep belief networks, improving MNIST results and remaining competitive on Caltech-101.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient optimization uses randomly sampled data to estimate a gradient instead of computing it from the entire dataset. This saves computation per update, but a highly variable estimate can make optimization bounce around and converge slowly. The paper develops a general approach for reducing that variability using control variates.

The control variate is constructed from data statistics, including low-order moments. Those statistics can be calculated beforehand or estimated online. The approach uses this statistical information to reduce gradient noise, addressing the quality of the stochastic update while retaining the sample-based optimization framework.

The authors demonstrate constructions for two different problems: maximum a posteriori estimation in logistic regression, which is convex, and stochastic variational inference for latent Dirichlet allocation, which is non-convex. On both, the proposed approach converges faster and performs better than the classical approach. The examples show that the same variance-reduction idea can be useful in both optimization settings, with its concrete construction adapted to each problem.
neurips-2013-variance-reduction-for-stoc.tldr: Control variates built from data statistics reduce stochastic gradient noise and improve convergence in logistic regression and latent Dirichlet allocation.
